title: How EPFO’s new plan for PF withdrawals will work
content_html:
The key proposal on the agenda pertains to allowing a systematic withdrawal plan with monthly payouts at the time of retirement instead of lump sum withdrawal of the entire corpus. Photo: File
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The Central Board of Trustees (CBT) of the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) held its 240th meeting on Thursday (November 19) to discuss the key proposal of allowing a systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) with periodic payouts at the time of retirement instead of lump sum withdrawal of the entire corpus.

The EPFO also eased withdrawal rules by reducing the minimum balance requirement to 10% from 25% — a reversal of its earlier decision that had faced social media backlash and criticism from Opposition parties at the time of its announcement last year. There was also relief provided to those who opt for premature final settlement, especially after being unemployed, with a reduction in the waiting period for final provident fund settlement.

Members will now once again be allowed to claim premature final settlement of their provident fund after remaining unemployed for two months, instead of the 12-month waiting period introduced in October 2025 for full withdrawal. The minimum waiting period for final pension withdrawal will remain 36 months.

Systematic withdrawal plan

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The SWP proposes to allow retiring members to retain their savings within the EPF ecosystem, continue earning EPF interest, and receive post-retirement income without surrendering ownership of the residual corpus. Multiple withdrawal options are proposed to be provided to EPF subscribers: full systematic withdrawal, or partial lump-sum withdrawal with SWP for the balance, or interest-only withdrawal models. Under the SWP, the retiring members will be able to withdraw their accumulated PF savings at regular intervals, such as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, based on their preference.

The facility would be “entirely voluntary, with no compulsion on members to opt for withdrawals”, the Ministry of Labour and Employment said in a statement. The option may also be extended to eligible family members and beneficiaries, for greater flexibility and financial security for the family. “This aims to ensure stable post-retirement income, reduce reinvestment risks, strengthen fund sustainability and facilitate the extension of social security coverage to gig and platform workers,” it said.

Also, the SWP proposes to allow the members to make voluntary contributions directly into their EPF accounts through digital channels designated by EPFO independent of employer payroll systems. Such contributions would not require employer matching contributions and would be credited directly into the member’s provident fund account.

The retiree will also be permitted to terminate the SWP and withdraw the remaining balance at any stage. It is also proposed that the spouse or nominee rights will be continued for the SWP for the balance EPF corpus of the member on same terms in the event of death of the member during the SWP tenure.

Story continues below this ad

At present, EPFO members can withdraw 100% of their accumulated provident fund balance on retirement at the age of 58. Members with at least 10 years of eligible service can separately receive a monthly pension under the Employees’ Pension Scheme.

Around 6.32 lakh members above the age of 55 possess provident fund savings exceeding Rs 5 lakh and are expected to benefit from the SWP. The EPFO, which has over 8 crore active contributing members and over 34 crore total members, manages a retirement corpus of nearly Rs 32 lakh crore.

As per internal estimates listed in the SWP proposal, the periodic withdrawals by a member may generate higher monthly payouts when compared with comparable bank fixed deposit and annuity arrangements.

Coverage for gig, informal workers

The proposal will also introduce a framework to allow direct voluntary contributions and third-party micro-contributions (such as customer tips) directly into EPF accounts through Universal Account Number (UAN)-linked digital payment mechanisms, completely independent of traditional employer payroll systems. This would enable informal and incidental income streams to be converted into long-term retirement savings. Such contributions, however, will be subject to limits prescribed in the Income-tax Act and will be governed by rules and procedures specified by the CBT.

Story continues below this ad
Also read | EPFO launches WhatsApp service to check PF balance, passbook, last five transactions

“This SWP scheme intends to provide flexible options to the member for enhancing his corpus in PF by means of voluntary contributions through payroll, direct additional contributions other than payroll and third-party micro-contributions. The proposed architecture of the SWP scheme provides for the possibility that the scheme may be extended to facilitate social security coverage and retirement savings mechanisms for gig workers, platform workers, construction workers, domestic workers, street vendors, home-based workers, among others,” an official said.

Investment proposal for AIFs

The EPFO’s Board gave also in-principle approval to allow investment of up to 3% of fresh accretion (annual inflows) in eligible Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), within the existing overall investment ceiling, initially through government-backed entities. Investment in government-anchored funds under National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) and through “Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0” scheme managed by the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) will be in focus.

AIF means any fund incorporated in India in the form of a trust or a company or a limited liability partnership or a body corporate which – (i) is a privately pooled investment vehicle which collects funds from investors, whether Indian or foreign, for investing it in accordance with a defined investment policy for the benefit of its investors; and (ii) is not covered under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, SEBI (Collective Investment Schemes) Regulations, 1999 or any other regulations of the Board.

Also in Explained | What EPFO wage ceiling hike means for employees, why some have criticised it

The Secretary, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) had written to the EPFO in September 2026 inviting EPFO to examine participation in the Fund of Funds for Startups 2.0 through an appropriate co-investment or contribution structure, subject to EPFO’s applicable investment framework and requisite approvals, The Indian Express had learnt.

Story continues below this ad

Also, the EPFO’s Investment Committee had earlier discussed the proposal for investment in AIFs, where the risk-return profile of AIFs versus Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) or Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) as an asset class was highlighted. While InvITs are pooled investment vehicles that own and manage operational infrastructure assets such as highways and power transmission lines, REITs pertain to income-generating commercial real estate such as office parks and warehouses.

The committee members said that AIFs — particularly those investing in start-ups and venture capital — have a significantly different risk-return profile and do not necessarily generate regular income. The committee then gave an in-principle approval for investment in AIFs limited to 3% of fresh accretions during a financial year.

title: Anthropic’s stock market debut marks many firsts. Will it boost a struggling AI sector?
content_html:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind Claude, priced its IPO at $83 a share when it listed on the Nasdaq, well above the expected range, and ended up selling far more shares than planned. The company has seen its value jump to as much as $1.5 trillion as its shares are set to start trading from Thursday, already making it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

There are many other interesting firsts. Anthropic’s stock market debut will make it the first wholly AI-focused company to go public, at a time when the fast-growing sector faces multiple questions over the amount of money being poured into the technology.

Advertisement

What is remarkable is that this company has been in existence for just around five years. And to put the listing performance in perspective, Anthropic’s valuation is already more than the cumulative market cap of the top 10 Indian companies.

How big is Anthropic’s stock market debut?

The listing would mean Anthropic’s seven co-founders are set to become ‘decabillionaires’ (wealth exceeding $10 billion). Since Anthropic’s shares were oversubscribed to the tune of more than 10 times ahead of the listing, its valuation could surge past its target when trading kicks off Thursday.

title: Power shortage looms: Why states are flocking to spot market as coal stocks dip
content_html:
India faces growing power shortage concerns as declining coal stocks and inadequate thermal capacity raise questions over electricity supply ahead of next summer. (Magnific)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

A looming power shortage, triggered by a shortage of baseload thermal capacity and mounting worries over coal stocks, has spurred a flurry of high-level meetings at the Centre.

With the states now being directed to secure electricity at all costs, the worries about an impending electricity shock early next summer have triggered a panic reaction that is reverberating across the country’s electricity ecosystem.

Multiple states are turning to short-term power procurement tenders, mostly at exorbitant prices, to secure additional electricity for the coming months and guard against potential shortages, particularly during evening peak hours.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Data from the Ministry of Power’s DEEP (Discovery of Efficient Electricity Price) portal showed that tenders have been floated for power procurement by at least five states and private distribution utilities for additional power during the months of January, February, March, April, May and June-July next year. The states seeking to procure additional power include Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Rajasthan and Gujarat.

Uttar Pradesh is also learnt to be vying for securing additional power ahead of the state elections early next year.

Here is why power prices are surging in short-term tenders, how sharply coal stocks have depleted at thermal plants, and what past policy missteps left the grid vulnerable.

Why power prices are soaring in short-term tenders

Private distribution companies, including Noida Power Company Ltd and Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd (AEML), have also floated tenders. Prices discovered in some of these tenders have touched Rs 19-20 per unit, significantly higher than the price caps applicable in power exchanges.

Story continues below this ad
Also in Explained | FPIs pump record $11.3 billion in November: What drove this comeback?

While the cap on spot prices is Rs 10 per unit, prices can go up to Rs 20 per unit in the specialised High Price Day-Ahead Market (HP-DAM). Also, amid a decline in coal stocks, the government is also discussing measures to expand coal storage capacity at thermal power plants beyond the prescribed normative requirement, The Indian Express has learnt.

While the normative requirement is around 59 million tonnes (mt), thermal power plants currently have the capacity to store up to 80 mt, equivalent to about 30 days of consumption. Discussions are also underway on doubling this capacity to 160 mt, which would provide up to 60 days of coal stocks. However, such an expansion would require additional storage space at thermal power plants.

While sporadic instances of rains may have helped mitigate the shortage this year, there are concerns about a problem from early next summer. Grid India’s daily frequency profile data is showing even during these somewhat lean demand months real-time frequency is falling to below the mandated lower limit of 49.9 HZ even during solar hours (when solar generation is available). The situation during the non-solar hours (evenings, when solar generation is not available) is even more precipitous.

Coal stocks at thermal plants fall sharply, raising shortage fears

Story continues below this ad

The increased dependence on coal-based generation has put pressure on coal inventories at thermal power plants. Stocks declined by around 66% between April and September this year, compared with a fall of around 23% during the same period last year, when inventories dropped from 55.2 mt at the beginning of April to 42.6 mt by September end.

The corresponding declines during the same period were 31.8% in 2024 and 36.8% in 2023.

As of November 15, coal inventory at domestic coal-based power plants stood at 20.79 mt, down from around 55 mt at the beginning of April. Officials in the Ministry of Power have also maintained that rebuilding coal stocks ahead of next summer is among the key priorities given the current circumstances.

The fresh directive to ramp up coal storage capacity comes in this backdrop.

Story continues below this ad

How past policy decisions left India vulnerable to a power crunch

Internally, the Union Power Ministry’s planning body — the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) — has already given a broader call for a reassessment of planned coal-based capacity additions, even as the country continues to expand its renewable energy capacity.

Also Read | ‘Very wrong signal to investors’: Behind Vedanta’s Anil Agarwal’s message to govt on ONGC transfer

With India staring at a power shortage, CEA chairperson Ghanshyam Prasad had flagged the need to to add 105-150 gigawatts (GW) of coal-based power capacity by 2035, significantly higher than the 97 GW currently planned, at a meeting on October 13.

India’s focus on rapid expansion of renewables in the absence of energy storage systems is making the electricity grid increasingly unstable. The issue is compounded by a policy decision from around ten years ago to scale down thermal expansion, which provides critical baseload support to the grid during evenings in summer months, when solar generation dips and demand remains high.

The Union Power Ministry’s National Electricity Plan (2017-22) had ruled out fresh thermal capacity additions beyond 2022, apart from the 50 GW of under-construction projects. It mainly focused on scaling up renewables. Additionally, imported coal-based projects were actively discouraged, primarily in the wake of spiralling global coal prices.

Story continues below this ad

Since the planning misstep of 2016-17, some corrective measures have been taken: a renewed push for nuclear generation in fleet mode, a belated drive to add large thermal capacities, importing coal to restart idle plants, and renewed policy pivots such as the CEA’s directive from last year that mandated storage for all new solar projects.

‘Very wrong signal to investors’: Behind Vedanta’s Anil Agarwal’s message to govt on ONGC transfer
content_html:
Water jets are sprayed on the rig during containment operations after a gas leakage was reported at an ONGC well near NH-216 in Geddada village (ANI Video Grab)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Industrialist and chairman of the Vedanta group on Tuesday (November 17) cautioned that the Centre’s move to transfer operations of one of its oil and gas blocks to public sector major Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) could send a “very wrong signal” to investors at a time when the government is looking to boost private and foreign investment in India’s hydrocarbon exploration and production sector. He also urged the government to maintain regulatory stability.

Behind Agarwal’s comments, which he made through a post on LinkedIn, is a hydrocarbon block that the government asked ONGC to take over, and the ongoing legal dispute around it.

The block Agarwal was referring to is the offshore Cambay basin oil and gas block CB-OS-02, which is off the Gujarat coast. Vedanta held a 40% participating interest in the block, and was its operator as well. ONGC held 50% in it and Invenire Petrodyne held the remaining 10%. But ONGC has now taken over the block, after the government refused to extend Vedanta’s application for an extension of its production sharing contract (PSC), and the Delhi High Court upheld that decision.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The block in question and the story so far

The production sharing contract for the block expired on June 29, 2023, although Vedanta and its joint venture partners had applied for an extension on June 28, 2021, under the government’s 2017 PSC extension policy. The government, however, rejected Vedanta’s request in September last year and ordered the block to be handed over to ONGC.

Within days, Vedanta moved the Delhi High Court against the government’s decision. But on July 22 this year, its writ petition was dismissed by a single-judge bench of the court, which removed the interim stay that had earlier maintained status quo on the matter. Although Vedanta has appealed against the order before a division bench of the Delhi High Court, ONGC took control of the block and applied for a petroleum lease on July 28.

“Company (ONGC) has taken effective control of the said block with effect from July 22, 2026, consequent to Government’s directive to take control of the block. On July 22, 2026 Vedanta Limited has challenged the said order in Divisional Bench of the Hon’ble High Court of Delhi, and the matter is currently under adjudication.

The ultimate outcome of the litigation and its consequential impact, if any, cannot presently be determined,” ONGC said in a recent regulatory filing.

Story continues below this ad

“…subsequent to decision of Single Bench of Delhi High Court, ONGC has taken over the Block. The company (Vedanta Oil and Gas) has filed an appeal against the said dismissal before the Division Bench of the Delhi High Court. The hearings have concluded on 1st October and the matter is reserved for judgement,” Vedanta Oil and Gas said in a regulatory filing.

It added that in view of the developments, absence of a valid PSC, and the resulting uncertainty regarding recoverability of assets and receivables relating to the block, it has recognised an impairment charge of about Rs 379 crore during the first quarter of the current financial year. Vedanta also stopped recognising revenue and related expenses from the block from July 22.

Anil Agarwal’s objections

“Recently, our running field has been given to ONGC which will send a very wrong signal to investors. We are seeing such great energy and enthusiasm from global investors.

This is the time to keep the policy hand steady and not disrupt any existing operator. That shall go a long way in building and boosting global investor confidence. Let us all together make a determined move to increase domestic production and reduce oil and gas imports drastically,” Agarwal said in his LinkedIn post.

Story continues below this ad

“India is on the verge of something big in oil and gas. Like Guayana was ten years ago. We have a world-class policy ecosystem and a willingness to move from approvals to self-certification. Vedanta Oil and Gas, India’s largest private sector producer is committing USD 5 billion in investments to scale up production to 300,000-500,000 barrels per day. We have already moved into the deep sea Samudra Manthan programme,” he said.

Also Read | E20 petrol row: Why Karnataka’s allegations could reignite the ethanol blending debate

The timing of the developments pertaining to the CB-OS-02 block and Agarwal’s comments are significant as they come amid the government’s push to increase participation from the private sector and global oil and gas firms in India’s upstream oil and gas sector. India is the world’s third-largest consumer of crude oil and depends on imports to meet over 88% of its requirement. It is also a major importer of liquefied natural gas (LNG) with an import dependency of about 50%.

A series of oil and gas block auctions have been held over the years, but the interest from global investors has been largely absent. Among domestic private sector investors, Vedanta has been the biggest in terms of bidding for new blocks, and the auctions have largely seen participation from public sector oil and gas companies.

The Samudra Manthan scheme, or the National Offshore Exploration Scheme, which Agarwal referred to is an ambitious Rs 84,084-crore programme that the green-lighted about three-and-a-half months ago.

Story continues below this ad

The scheme will provide financial support for exploratory drilling in deep-sea and ultra-deep-sea areas and support building of common infrastructure for production of discovered hydrocarbons in offshore areas, apart from funding offshore data acquisition and developing hydrocarbon manufacturing and services zones. The Rs 84,084-crore outlay is for implementation till financial year 2030-31.

The Centre expects the Samudra Manthan scheme to catalyse reserve accretion of over 600 million tonnes of oil and oil equivalent gas (mtoe), while stimulating significant investments across the oil and gas exploration and production value chain.

The scheme will provide support of up to 50% of drilling cost or Rs 675 crore, whichever is lower, for every well drilled in deep-sea and ultra-deep-sea areas. Drilling at such depths is an expensive proposition, costing between $100 million and $250 million per well, as per industry estimates.

It is also risky as the drilling activity may not lead to any oil or natural gas discovery. In certain cases, even if hydrocarbons are discovered, it may not be commercially viable to exploit them. The scheme, officials expect, will mitigate some of the investment risks for upstream oil and gas players, and increase investment into the sector.

content_html:
The Donald Trump administration has announced sweeping new restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies from accessing advanced American chips through data centres located outside China, as Washington faces growing questions over the effectiveness of its technology export controls.

The new regulations, announced by the US Commerce Department on Monday (November 16), seek to close a significant loophole in America’s restrictions on advanced AI chips. New restrictions target overseas data centres and remote computing

Importantly, the restrictions also cover companies whose ultimate parent organisation is based in these countries, seeking to prevent Chinese entities from circumventing the rules through subsidiaries registered elsewhere.

The rule sets a threshold of more than 12 million aggregate Total Processing Performance (TPP), a measure of computing capability, for restricted remote access. It also covers computing capacity distributed across interconnected data centres.

Separately, Washington has introduced additional licensing requirements for exports of advanced semiconductors to five countries — Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil — which it identifies as presenting a higher risk of chip diversion. Certain shipments to US-headquartered companies are exempt, subject to reporting requirements.

Existing data centres providing restricted computing services will have 90 days from the rule’s effective date to obtain the necessary licences to continue doing so. The regulations exempt commercial recommendation systems, including those used by e-commerce and social media companies.

The rule also formally rescinds the Biden administration’s broader AI Diffusion Rule, which was never enforced, replacing it with more targeted restrictions.

Washington’s concerns extend beyond the physical movement of chips

For several years, the US has sought to limit China’s access to advanced semiconductors, arguing that the same powerful processors used to develop commercial AI applications could also strengthen Beijing’s military and intelligence capabilities.

These chips are critical to training increasingly sophisticated AI models, and Washington has sought to preserve America’s technological advantage by restricting China’s access to the most advanced hardware.

Also Read | Jensen Huang resigns: Why his exit from Nvidia will be a test for the AI boom

However, restrictions on the physical shipment of processors have created another challenge for US authorities. Chinese companies can potentially access powerful American chips without importing them, simply by purchasing computing services from overseas data centres.

The Commerce Department said the new controls were necessary because advanced AI systems could be used to develop sophisticated weapons, conduct cyber-espionage, disrupt critical systems and support military operations.

Nvidia’s Megaspeed controversy has intensified scrutiny

The announcement comes against the backdrop of growing scrutiny of Nvidia and the Commerce Department over their handling of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based provider of computing services with operations linked to Southeast Asia.

Megaspeed has faced allegations that it helped Chinese companies access restricted Nvidia processors, potentially undermining Washington’s export controls.

The controversy intensified following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, who previously worked with Megaspeed and was suspected by US intelligence officials of having connections to Beijing.

Also Read | Jensen Huang-Alice Huang affair: How the Nvidia scandal became a US security concern

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12. However, US authorities have not concluded that Alice Huang was engaged in espionage, and Beijing has rejected the allegations.

Singaporean authorities have separately investigated Megaspeed since February 2025 over possible false declarations relating to server purchases. On Monday, the US Commerce and Justice departments disclosed that Washington had initiated its own investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 over potential export-control violations.

Megaspeed has maintained that it complies with applicable laws, including US export-control requirements.

The episode has also triggered political scrutiny in Washington, with lawmakers questioning whether the administration had done enough to prevent American technology from reaching China.

Fresh evidence raises doubts over the effectiveness of export controls

The restrictions follow research published last week by Unemployment Labs, which found evidence suggesting that several advanced Chinese AI models were developed using Nvidia’s export-restricted Blackwell processors.

The researchers identified numerical fingerprints in models developed by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group that were consistent with the use of Blackwell hardware.

While the findings do not conclusively establish how or where the chips were accessed, they add to concerns that American export restrictions have not entirely prevented Chinese companies from obtaining advanced computing capabilities.

Separately, research organisation Epoch AI has estimated that around two million advanced AI chips entered China during 2024 and 2025 through arrangements designed to conceal their final destination.

title: Dhoni retires: 5 captaincy masterstrokes that shaped CSK’s title-winning finals
content_html:
Mahendra Singh Dhoni's playing career in the IPL ended on Tuesday after he was appointed the mentor of his franchise Chennai Super Kings. (PTI)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

After 278 matches, 235 of them as captain, 5,439 runs and 24 half-centuries, MS Dhoni has called time on his career as an Indian Premier League (IPL) player. On Tuesday (November 17), Chennai Super Kings announced that their five-time title-winning captain would assume a new role as the team’s mentor.

What defined Dhoni’s tenure at CSK, however, was never merely the runs he accumulated or the sixes he sent soaring into the stands. It was the subtle, delicate decisions not accounted for in the scorecards or statisticians’ notes, but left an indelible mark on the game.

We revisit five such moments — one from each of the five IPL finals in which CSK emerged victorious.

2010: The straight mid-off

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

CSK had come close to a maiden title in each of the first two editions but couldn’t cross the finish line. In 2010, it seemed they finally would, with Mumbai Indians reduced to 114/6 after 17 overs while chasing 168. But Kieron Pollard smashed 22 runs off Doug Bollinger’s next over to drag Mumbai back into the game.

With CSK defending 27 off 7 and Albie Morkel bowling the penultimate over, a fielding tweak from Dhoni earned them their maiden crown. He directed Matthew Hayden at mid-off to go straighter and stand just behind Morkel. Commentating on air, Sunil Gavaskar remarked, “It’s one of the straightest mid-offs you will ever see.” Pollard’s propensity to hit straight proved his undoing, as he was caught at exactly that position.

2011: Ashwin with the new ball

Royal Challengers Bengaluru might not have waited 18 years for a title had it not been for a Dhoni masterclass in the 2011 final. The season belonged to Chris Gayle, who had established himself as T20 cricket’s most destructive batter with 608 runs at a strike rate of 183.13. Gayle had few weaknesses at the time, apart from his vulnerability against off-spin.

Also Read | In Ranchi, parents wanted children to become docs, engineers before Dhoni arrived

Dhoni gave the new ball to Ravichandran Ashwin while defending 205, and on just the fourth delivery of the chase, Gayle fell to an ill-fated cut that took the edge and landed in Dhoni’s gloves.

2018: The backward square leg

Story continues below this ad
Karan Sharma of CSK celebrates after the wicket of Kane Williamson against SRH during the IPL 2018 final against SRH at Wankhede stadium. (Express Photo by Kevin DSouza)

CSK’s seven-year wait for a third title ended in 2018 with an eight-wicket win over Sunrisers Hyderabad. Batting first, SRH were approaching 150 in the 17th over, with captain Kane Williamson having laid the foundation with a 36-ball 47. The onus then fell on Deepak Hooda to provide a strong finish.

Also in Explained | Ball tampering in cricket: The science, history and methods behind it

With Lungi Ngidi bowling, Dhoni placed Dhruv Shorey at backward square leg, and Hooda holed out to him just two deliveries later. Ngidi would go on to acknowledge the role Dhoni’s clever field placements played in CSK’s win.

2021: Thakur’s early return

Chasing 193 in the 2021 final, Kolkata Knight Riders seemed to be cruising towards their third IPL title at 88/0 after 10 overs, with Shubman Gill and Venkatesh Iyer once again working wonders at the top. In the 11th over, Dhoni went back to Shardul Thakur, who had conceded 11 in his first over and would usually be saved for the death. It proved the right call, as Thakur dismissed both Gill and Iyer in that over.

2023: Chahar’s final over

CSK team lift IPL 2023 trophy beating Gujarat Titans at Narendra Modi stadium in Ahmedabad on May 29, 2023. Express photo by Nirmal Harindran, 29-05-2023, Ahmedabad *** Local Caption *** CSK team lift IPL 2023 trophy beating Gujarat Titans at Narendra Modi stadium in Ahmedabad on Monday. (Express photo by Nirmal Harindran)

At 124/1 after 13 overs, Gujarat Titans had exactly the start they wanted in the 2023 final. Even so, Dhoni called on Deepak Chahar to bowl his fourth and final over, despite the seamer having conceded 31 without a wicket in his first three.

Story continues below this ad

It proved to be the downfall of a well-set Wriddhiman Saha, who had already brought up his half-century. Trying to slog a leg-cutter, the keeper edged it to his Chennai counterpart, and the wicket proved crucial given how well Saha was batting.

title: Quad leaders meet in Manila: Why the grouping matters amid Indo-Pacific tensions
content_html:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi poses for a group photo with QUAD Leaders- US President Donald Trump, Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of the ASEAN-India Summit and East Asia Summit, in Manila on Tuesday. (DD/ANI)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Prime Minister Narendra Modi met US President Donald Trump, Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and Australian PM Anthony Albanese at the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit for the first meeting in two years of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) group of Indo-Pacific countries.

This will be Trump’s first Quad leaders’ meeting since beginning his second term in January 2025.

What is the Quad? 

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, or Quad, originated as an informal partnership comprising India, Japan, Australia and the US to coordinate disaster relief operations after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

In 2007, Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe proposed a political framework for this grouping.

Right from the outset, the nascent group lacked cohesiveness among its members. Critics argued that they had few strategic aims in common other than an opposition to Chinese territorial assertions in the Indo-Pacific region. China itself accused it of being little more than an anti-China bloc.

After losing its initial momentum, the group was revived nearly a decade later during Trump’s first presidential term in 2017 and broadened its objectives when faced with the rising China challenge.

Why the Quad is not a military alliance like NATO

Unlike a typical multilateral organisation like the United Nations or the European Union, the Quad has no organised physical presence. It does not have a secretariat or a permanent decision-making body.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | How 2 major summits this week point to balance & bargain strategy in big-power diplomacy

It has, however, focused on expanding existing agreements among member countries and highlighting their shared values.

As an informal grouping, the Quad also lacks provisions for collective defence (unlike NATO’s defining Article 5), relying instead on coordination, strategic dialogue, and joint military exercises to demonstrate alignment.

Questions have also arisen about the Quad’s long-term strategic coherence, particularly as member countries balance economic ties with China alongside security concerns in the Indo-Pacific.

While the Quad was revived during Trump’s first term in 2017, there was ambiguity over its longterm direction given changes in political leadership in member countries and debates over burden-sharing. As a result, India, Japan, and Australia have gained a greater role in sustaining the grouping’s momentum.

Story continues below this ad

What are the Quad’s objectives in the Indo-Pacific?

The grouping took a step towards formalisation in 2020, when the trilateral India-US-Japan Malabar naval exercises expanded to include Australia, marking the first joint military exercises among the four countries in over a decade.

In March 2021, the Quad leaders met virtually amid the Covid pandemic and released a joint statement titled ‘The Spirit of the Quad,’ outlining the group’s approach and objectives.

The first in-person meeting of Quad leaders was also that year in Washington DC.

The Quad’s agenda has since expanded to include resilient supply chains, critical and emerging technologies, cybersecurity, cooperation in semiconductors and critical minerals, and energy security. Recent geopolitical disruptions and the resulting supply chain vulnerabilities have further sharpened the grouping’s focus on economic resilience and strategic coordination.

Story continues below this ad
China This Week | Spotlight on Chinese spying in Jensen Huang saga, and a Xi-Trump-Putin meeting

Given growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific, maritime security remains central to Quad’s outlook, alongside concerns over freedom of navigation and member states’ anxieties about China’s expanding military and maritime presence in the region. The four countries have also coordinated on disaster relief, climate resilience, and health security initiatives.

Quad members have also indicated a willingness to expand the partnership through a so-called Quad Plus that would include South Korea, New Zealand, and Vietnam, amongst others. However, as Major General G G Dwivedi explained in May 2026, Seoul’s focus on the Korean Peninsula and Hanoi’s policy of avoiding military alliances may limit their participation.
